newsitem.title: JORDAN: EU parliamentarians to lobby against Israel accord.
newsitem.headline: EU parliamentarians to lobby against Israel accord.

text.p: A group of EU parliamentarians said on Saturday they would try to block ratification of a European-Israeli economic pact in protest at what they called Israeli obstruction of Middle East peace efforts.

Sir Robert Hicks, co-chairman of the Parliamentary Association for Euro-Arab Cooperation, said the association would try to stop the accord, agreed in November 1995 with Israel's previous Labour government, from being carried out.

Implementation next January of the agreement, which would upgrade trade and economic cooperation between Europe and Israel, was linked "to progress and encouragement of the peace process", Hicks told a meeting of the Euro-Arab Parliamentary Dialogue held in the Jordanian parliament.
"It is quite clear to us as European parliamentarians that unfortunately one side is not adhering, not only to the spirit of that arrangement but indeed also to the word," Hicks said.
He said the European delegates had decided "to do what we could in our own national parliaments to postpone ratification of the Euro-Mediterranean agreement between the European Union and Israel."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came to power in May on a platform which rejects trading Arab land in return for peace. Talks with Syria and Lebanon have stopped and progress on the Palestinian self-rule accords have stalled.
Hicks said the action would send a message to Netanyahu that "European parliamentarians are not happy with the present policies adopted by the Israeli government with respect to the peace process."

He said the decision to lobby for the postponement was taken by delegates from 14 European national assemblies and the EU parliament who believed Middle East peace talks had come to a stop "largely as a result of a change of government in Israel".

Jordan's Crown Prince Hassan criticised Europe's interest in the Middle East as lukewarm and ill-coordinated. The Middle East "was no longer on the screen" as Europe looked further east towards Asia for business and trade, he said.
He also criticized those who saw the region merely as a lucrative bazaar to sell arms in return for cheap oil.

"At the turn of the century the (European) emphasis was very much on zones of interest, on oil, as it (remains) at the turn of the 21st century -- vested interest in oil and weapons, not vested interest in politics for people."
He said the only hope for the Middle East was if governments within and from outside the region dropped their own individual agendas and searched seriously for peace.
"Then and only then can we hope for an agenda at the end of this century that may just look less worrisome than it did at the end of the 19th century," Prince Hassan said.
Jordan signed a peace accord with Israel in 1994 ending a 46-year state of war.
